meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only source of knowledge is experience'?
meta.ogDescription: Popularly credited to Einstein, but the Einstein Archives says no. It’s a folk version of Lockean empiricism, documented as early as 1896.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — a stock empiricist maxim
answer.authorDates: Empiricist commonplace · near-verbatim wording documented by 1896; idea traceable to John Locke (1632–1704)
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Albert Einstein ever wrote or said this, and the Hebrew University’s Albert Einstein Archives confirms it is not one of his quotations ↗. It is a folk distillation of classic empiricism — the notion that knowledge comes ‘from experience’ goes back to John Locke, and the near-verbatim phrasing appears in an 1896 magazine essay, decades before it was pinned on Einstein.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Not one of Einstein’s quotations (Einstein Archives)

source.excerpt: Information is not knowledge. The only source of knowledge is experience.
trail: The Hebrew University’s Albert Einstein Archives says this is not one of Einstein’s identifiable quotations ↗.
The near-verbatim phrasing is documented in an 1896 essay — “our only source of knowledge is experience” (Arthur J. Pillsbury, “The Final Word,” Overland Monthly) — per the same Wikiquote record ↗.
The idea itself paraphrases John Locke’s empiricism — knowledge drawn ‘from experience’ — also cited in the Wikiquote entry ↗.
Einstein’s genuine, sourced view was more nuanced — see his 1933 lecture On the Method of Theoretical Physics ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the tidy version Einstein never wrote
source.excerptNote: What Einstein actually said — in his 1933 Herbert Spencer Lecture at Oxford — was far more careful: “Pure logical thinking can give us no knowledge whatsoever of the world of experience; all knowledge about reality begins with experience and terminates in it.” He also stressed that theory can never be derived from experience alone.
source.rightsNote: Because the maxim has no verified modern author and its wording predates 1929, it is effectively in the public domain and free to quote — just don’t credit it to Einstein.

author.name: John Locke
author.heading: John Locke & the roots of empiricism
author.bio: John Locke was an English philosopher whose An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) argued that the mind starts as a blank slate and draws all its ‘materials of reason and knowledge’ from experience. That thesis — empiricism — is the true ancestor of the modern one-liner, though Locke never phrased it as the tidy aphorism now hung on Einstein. Ironically, Einstein himself rejected pure empiricism, insisting that scientific theories are ‘free inventions of the human spirit’ that cannot be derived from experience alone.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared ‘Einstein’ quotes online — on posters, mugs, and slide decks — but the attribution does not hold up.

items.why: According to Barbara Wolff of the Hebrew University’s Albert Einstein Archives, this is not one of Einstein’s identifiable quotations ↗. No source in his writings has been located, and the near-verbatim wording appears in an 1896 essay — before Einstein was known.
Locke is the real intellectual source of the idea — knowledge drawn ‘from experience’ in his 1689 Essay — but he never wrote this exact sentence; it is a modern condensation, as noted on Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no evidence Einstein ever said it: the line is a modern distillation of Lockean empiricism whose earliest documented wording is an 1896 magazine essay — and Einstein’s own epistemology actually resisted the claim that experience is the only source of knowledge (1933 lecture ↗).

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks — and why it’s ironic
lead: The line is irresistible because it sounds like Einstein: crisp, humble, pro-experiment. That surface fit is exactly why it spread. But the Hebrew University’s Einstein Archives ↗ lists it among quotations Einstein did not say, and its near-verbatim wording is documented in an obscure 1896 magazine essay — well before Einstein was famous.

The deeper irony is that Einstein’s real epistemology pushed against the slogan. He agreed that knowledge ‘begins with experience,’ but insisted, per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗, that scientific theories are ‘free inventions of the human spirit’ that can never be derived from experience alone.
context.detailsSummary: Read Einstein’s actual words on experience
detailsBody: In his 1933 Herbert Spencer Lecture at Oxford, On the Method of Theoretical Physics, Einstein said: ‘Pure logical thinking can give us no knowledge whatsoever of the world of experience; all knowledge about reality begins with experience and terminates in it.’ The circulated maxim keeps the ‘begins with experience’ half and drops Einstein’s crucial qualification — that experience is a starting point and a test, not the whole of knowing.

The underlying thesis is far older than either man’s celebrity: John Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) already answered the question of where the mind gets its materials of knowledge ‘in one word, from experience.’ The Einstein version is a 20th-century rebranding of a 17th-century empiricist commonplace.
